Newly hatched Mangrove killifish emerge from their eggs at a remarkably small size, with a total length at birth of just 0.51 centimeters [Lb = 0.51 centimeters]. This diminutive hatchling size is characteristic of many killifish species, reflecting a developmental strategy where the yolk-sac larva relies on its endogenous yolk reserves for a period of several days before transitioning to exogenous feeding during the larval feeding commencement stage. During embryonic development, the duration of which can be highly variable due to the species' capacity for diapause, the age at birth has a recorded lower boundary of approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] when incubated at a stable temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This ability to arrest development, known as embryonic diapause, means that hatching can be delayed for up to 90 days under unfavorable conditions, a remarkable adaptation to the ephemeral pools and crab burrows the species inhabits. The yolk-sac larva, initially an endotrophic organism, undergoes yolk resorption over its first days of free-swimming life, during which it exhibits no exogenous feeding behavior.

As individuals progress through the yolk-sac larva stage and transition to exogenous feeding, their growth trajectory becomes highly dependent on resource availability and environmental conditions. Data from laboratory-reared populations indicate that individuals attain a total length of 1.7 centimeters [Lp = 1.7 centimeters] at the point of sexual maturation. This length at puberty is a key milestone in the species' life history, marking the onset of vitellogenesis for females and spermiation for males. Under the same thermal conditions of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the age at which these fish first become reproductively capable is recorded at 35 days after hatching [tR = 35 days after hatching]. The first spawning event typically follows soon after this developmental milestone is reached, though the precise interval can be modulated by social cues and the availability of suitable oviposition substrates, such as the inner surface of empty mangrove crab burrows.

The gonado-somatic index of iteroparous adults provides a detailed measure of their reproductive investment. For a specimen measuring 2.64 centimeters in total length, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 0.38% [GSI = 0.38%] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This value highlights the high investment in reproductive tissue characteristic of this species, reflecting the substantial resource allocation toward gametogenesis in a fish that inhabits unpredictable, temporary aquatic habitats where rapid exploitation of favorable conditions for reproduction is essential. At this same body length, a wet weight of 0.15 grams  has been recorded, providing a reference point for the relationship between length and mass in the sub-adult and adult size classes.

Longitudinal studies of captive-maintained individuals have provided robust estimates of the species' lifespan and maximal somatic growth. The asymptotic body size in this species is modest, with adults rarely exceeding approximately 4.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 4.5 centimeters] in total length. This modest final size is typical of the Rivulidae family, of which Kryptolebias marmoratus is a member, and is associated with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early and repeated reproduction. The maximum documented longevity for this species under controlled laboratory conditions is 4 years [am = 4 years], with temperature playing a critical role in the rate of aging; this figure was recorded in fish maintained at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. In the wild, senescence likely proceeds more rapidly due to the combined pressures of desiccation risk, predation, and resource limitation, though the ability to breathe air at the water's surface provides a notable advantage in hypoxic environments that would kill most other teleosts.

The reproductive biology of Kryptolebias marmoratus is defined by its unique sexual system, being one of only two known self-fertilizing hermaphroditic vertebrates. This trait has profound consequences for its demography and life history, allowing a single individual to colonize a new habitat and initiate a population. The length-weight relationship in this species demonstrates that individuals at the typical spawning size class of 2.64 centimeters achieve a body mass of 0.15 grams , consistent with the condition factor reported for other rivulids of comparable body length. The gonadosomatic index of approximately 0.38% [GSI = approximately 0.38%] was recorded at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This species' ability to produce clutches of eggs from a single, genetically identical parent has made it a celebrated model for studies of population genetics and the evolution of sex.
